system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old woman with primary central nervous system lymphoma, ulcerative colitis, asthma, and a history of DVT/PE was admitted for her 11th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy. She tolerated the treatment well, with expected transaminitis that resolved and manageable nausea. An MRI showed stable disease with no evidence of progression. She reported ongoing depressive symptoms, leading to a psychiatry consultation, initiation of citalopram, and referral for outpatient therapy. Social work was engaged to address financial stressors and disability resources. Her chronic right foot pain was reassessed, and gabapentin was uptitrated for better nocturnal control. She cleared methotrexate adequately and was discharged home in stable condition with plans to continue enoxaparin, resume mesalamine, and follow up with oncology in one month for the next cycle.
problems: Primary central nervous system lymphoma, unspecified site, extranodal and solid organ sites
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Antineoplastic and immunosuppressive drugs causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

Discharge Condition:

Discharge Instructions:

methotrexate chemotherapy for lymphoma in the brain.  You 
tolerated chemotherapy well.  We discussed your depression and

recommended that you need more care for your depression on a 
psychiatry inpatient unit.  After Discussion with Dr. ___,

two days prior to your next hospital admission for high dose

procedures.long_title: Injection or infusion of cancer chemotherapeutic substance

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your care team doctors. You’re here for your 12th cycle of high-dose methotrexate for your CNS lymphoma. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m okay physically. A bit tired, but no new pain or headaches. I just want to get through this cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you’re comfortable. I see your mom mentioned something important—about you taking a lot of oxycodone a few days ago. Can we talk about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… yeah. I was really overwhelmed. I took most of my pills, but I threw up that night. I didn’t mean to scare anyone. I just felt so stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad you’re honest. That sounds like a very hard moment. You’re not alone in this. We’ve asked Psychiatry to see you because your safety is our top priority.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t feel like hurting myself now. But I’ve been so sad. The chemo, losing my job, the pain… it’s a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes complete sense. You’ve been through so much. Psychiatry will help you find better ways to cope. We also want to support you with social work for the financial stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I do feel supported at home. My husband and mom are great. I just worry about money and insurance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll connect you with resources. For now, your chemo is scheduled for today. We’ll give you IV fluids to protect your kidneys and help clear the drug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I feel sick again like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nausea is common, but we’ll give you anti-nausea meds like ondansetron. You’ve tolerated it well before, so I’m hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chemotherapy infusion is starting now. It’ll take a few hours. Nurses will check on you often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My foot is aching a bit more today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve increased your gabapentin to 900mg three times a day to help with that. We’re stopping the oxycodone for now, given what happened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I don’t want to risk that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look stable. Liver enzymes are up a bit—this happens with methotrexate—but they should come down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually. It’s mild and temporary. We monitor it closely. You’re clearing the methotrexate well, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The Psychiatry team met with you yesterday. They think you’d benefit from a short inpatient stay for more support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was afraid they’d say that. But… maybe I do need more help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re increasing your citalopram to 40mg and adding lorazepam for anxiety at night. We’re also watching your heart rhythm since these meds can affect it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with monitoring. Your baseline EKG was normal. We’ll check it again soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your methotrexate levels are dropping well—0.15 now, down from 1.9 yesterday. That means your body is clearing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel more like myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also got your MRI results. Your lymphoma is still in stable remission. No progression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best news I’ve had in a while. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll repeat the MRI in a month. For your blood clot history, we’re switching from enoxaparin to aspirin 325mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and easier. But stop it two days before your next chemo admission to avoid interactions with the IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry has a bed for you at the inpatient unit. It’s a short stay—just until you’re feeling more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but I know I need this. Will my family be able to visit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. They’re part of your support. You’ll continue your gabapentin, aspirin, and other regular meds there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my asthma meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fluticasone-salmeterol, montelukast, and albuterol as needed. All continued.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to have a flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you doing emotionally today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still low, but talking to the psychiatrist helped. I’m scared of failing again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This isn’t failure. It’s courage to ask for help. You’re doing the right thing by getting more support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are coming down—ALT and AST are improving. That’s expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any other tests before I go to psych?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just one more methotrexate level to confirm it’s fully cleared. Then you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last methotrexate level is 0.05—essentially cleared. Great job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready for the next step, I think.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged for you to go to the psychiatric facility today. You’ll be there for about a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and back to oncology in a month for your next cycle and MRI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I restart mesalamine for my colitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once you’re home and stable. It was held during chemo due to interaction risks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And acyclovir?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re restarting that for herpes prevention. Take it three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before transfer. You’re alert, walking fine, and your labs are stable. Psych team is expecting you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared, but also hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely okay. You’re taking a brave step. We’ll follow up with you after your stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We never would. You’re strong, and you’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today you’ll be transferred to the psychiatric facility for continued care. Your discharge summary is ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take your new prescriptions: citalopram 40mg, aspirin, gabapentin 800mg three times a day, and lorazepam for anxiety at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And stop aspirin before next chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stop it two days before. Otherwise, keep everything going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old woman with primary central nervous system lymphoma, ulcerative colitis, asthma, and a history of DVT/PE was admitted for her 12th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy. She tolerated the treatment well, with expected mild transaminitis and manageable nausea. An MRI showed stable remission of her lymphoma. She disclosed a recent suicide attempt by oxycodone overdose, prompting a psychiatry consultation. Due to ongoing depressive symptoms and inadequate outpatient mental health resources, she was deemed unsafe for discharge home and arranged for transfer to an inpatient psychiatric facility. Her anticoagulation was changed from enoxaparin to aspirin per neuro-oncology recommendation. Gabapentin was increased for chronic right foot pain, and citalopram was uptitrated to 40mg daily. She cleared methotrexate adequately and was transferred to extended psychiatric care in stable condition.
